practices.name: Capital & Investment Advisory
practices.meta_title: Capital & Investment Advisory: The People Side of Deals
practices.meta_description: People-focused advisory for private equity, impact investors and acquirers: human capital diligence, value creation, integration and exit readiness.
practices.tagline: Evidence-based advice on the people who determine whether an investment thesis holds.
intro: Capital & Investment Advisory serves private equity sponsors, impact investors, family offices and corporate acquirers at the moments when people decisions carry the most financial weight: before signing, in the first hundred days, during integration and ahead of exit. We assess leadership teams, size organizational risk, build value creation plans that account for the workforce, and design measurement frameworks that investors and limited partners can trust. Our work sits alongside financial, commercial and legal diligence, and it answers the question those workstreams rarely address directly: can these people deliver this plan?

The people lens matters because most investment theses depend on human behavior. Revenue growth assumes a sales team that stays and performs. Margin expansion assumes managers who can redesign work without losing the operators who hold institutional knowledge. Integration assumes two cultures can agree on how decisions get made. When these assumptions fail, they tend to fail quietly and late. We bring them into view early, using structured interviews, people analytics and organizational diagnostics, so that sponsors can price risk, plan for it and act on it.

We also hold a conviction that responsible ownership and strong returns are compatible. Companies that treat employees fairly, serve customers well and earn the trust of their communities tend to be more resilient businesses. For impact and ESG-minded investors, we help translate that conviction into credible measurement, without overstating results or adding reporting burden that teams cannot sustain. We aim for evidence that boards, managers and stakeholders can all use.

themes.title: Leadership is the thesis
themes.body: Every deal model contains an implicit bet on a management team. We make that bet explicit by assessing leaders against the specific demands of the value creation plan, not against a generic competency list. Sponsors get a clear view of where the team is strong, where it is thin, and which gaps must be closed before the plan is credible.

themes.title: Workforce risk is financial risk
themes.body: Key person dependency, compensation misalignment, attrition in critical roles and unresolved cultural friction all show up eventually in EBITDA. We quantify these exposures where the data allows and describe them precisely where it does not, so that investment committees can weigh people risk alongside commercial and operational risk with the same rigor.

themes.title: Impact that holds up to scrutiny
themes.body: Impact and ESG claims face growing scrutiny from limited partners, regulators and the public. We help investors define outcomes that matter to employees, customers and communities, choose indicators they can collect consistently, and report with appropriate humility. The goal is measurement that informs decisions inside the portfolio, not only reporting that satisfies outside audiences.

practices.name: Leadership & Organization
practices.meta_description: Leadership and organization consulting grounded in evidence: org design, executive coaching, change, culture, succession and board governance.
practices.tagline: Stronger leaders, clearer structures and healthier cultures, built on evidence and designed with your people.
intro: Leadership & Organization helps executives, boards and senior teams build organizations that can carry out their strategy. We work on the structures, roles, decision rights and leadership capabilities that determine how work actually gets done, and on the culture that shapes how people behave when no one is directing them. Engagements range from focused executive coaching for a single leader to enterprise-wide organizational design and change programs that touch every level of a company or public agency.

The people lens matters here because organizations are not org charts. A structure that looks efficient on paper can slow decisions, overload middle managers and push talented people out. A leadership team that appears aligned in the boardroom can send conflicting signals to the front line. We use interviews, network analysis, surveys and operational data to see how the organization really functions, then co-design changes with the people who will live inside them. That combination of measurement and participation is what makes changes stick.

Our approach follows the same disciplined arc in every engagement: Listen, Measure, Design, Deliver, Sustain. We are direct about trade-offs, specific about accountabilities and realistic about the pace at which people can absorb change. We believe that leaders who build trust, clarity and fairness inside their organizations are better placed to serve customers and communities well, and that this is also the most reliable route to lasting performance.

themes.title: Clarity before capability
themes.body: Many leadership problems are design problems in disguise. When decision rights are ambiguous, spans of control are uneven or accountabilities overlap, even capable leaders struggle. We start by clarifying who decides what, how teams connect and where work gets stuck, so that development investments build on a structure that lets people succeed rather than compensate for one that does not.

themes.title: Change people can sustain
themes.body: Organizations can absorb only so much change at once. We sequence initiatives with attention to change load, equip managers to lead conversations with their teams, and track adoption through leading indicators rather than launch dates. This reduces change fatigue and gives leaders an honest picture of whether new ways of working are taking hold.

themes.title: Leadership as a system
themes.body: Individual leaders matter, but leadership is also a system of selection, development, succession, governance and team dynamics. We look at how these elements reinforce or undermine each other, from how the board oversees talent to how front-line supervisors are promoted, and design coherent improvements rather than isolated programs.

services.name: Private Equity Advisory
services.meta_title: Private Equity Advisory: Human Capital & Value Creation
services.meta_description: Private equity advisory focused on the people side of the deal cycle: diligence, management assessment, 100-day plans, integration and exit preparation.
services.summary: Human capital advice across the full deal cycle, from pre-signing diligence and management assessment through value creation, integration and exit.
services.lede: Private equity advisory for sponsors and operating partners who know that people execute the investment thesis. We bring evidence on leadership, workforce and culture to every stage of ownership, from diligence to exit.
challenge: Private equity firms have built sophisticated capabilities for financial, commercial and operational diligence, yet the human factors that drive most value creation plans are often assessed informally. Management teams are judged through a handful of meetings, workforce data arrives late and incomplete in the data room, and culture is treated as a soft topic until it becomes a hard problem. Holding periods are compressed, debt is expensive, and there is little room to discover in month nine that the CFO cannot scale or that the sales force is quietly leaving.

Operating partners carry much of this burden across many portfolio companies at once, often without dedicated human capital resources. They need consistent methods for assessing leaders, sizing workforce risk, setting people priorities in the 100-day plan and tracking progress through the hold period. Limited partners are also asking more pointed questions about talent practices, employee outcomes and responsible ownership. The firms that answer those questions credibly, with data rather than anecdote, are better positioned both to create value and to raise their next fund.

approach.title: Understand the thesis and the team
approach.body: We begin with the deal team and operating partners to understand the investment thesis, the value creation levers and the assumptions that depend on people. Where access allows, we conduct structured interviews with management, key employees and, when appropriate, customers, to understand how the business actually runs and where leadership capacity is concentrated or thin.

approach.title: Quantify people risk and opportunity
approach.body: We analyze workforce data for attrition patterns, compensation competitiveness, key person dependency, spans and layers, and labor cost structure. We assess leaders against the demands of the specific plan. The result is a fact base that sits alongside financial and commercial diligence and translates people findings into implications for the deal model.

approach.title: Build the people agenda
approach.body: We translate findings into a prioritized people agenda: leadership changes or additions, retention arrangements for critical talent, management incentive plan design principles, organizational changes and culture priorities. Each item links to a value creation lever, carries an owner and is sequenced realistically within the 100-day plan and the broader hold period.

approach.title: Support execution through the hold
approach.body: We work alongside portfolio company leaders and operating partners to execute: running executive searches with defined success profiles, facilitating leadership team alignment, supporting organizational redesign and guiding managers through change. Our role is to build capability inside the company, not to create permanent dependence on advisors.

approach.title: Track and report what matters
approach.body: We establish a small set of people metrics for board and sponsor review, such as regretted attrition in critical roles, leadership bench strength and engagement in key populations. These indicators feed board packs, LP reporting and, eventually, the exit narrative, giving sponsors evidence that the people agenda is delivering.

deliverables: Human capital risk assessment for the investment committee
Management team assessment against the value creation plan
People workstream for the 100-day plan
Key talent retention and incentive alignment recommendations
Portfolio people metrics framework for board reporting
Exit-ready leadership and organization narrative
outcomes: Investment committees weigh people risk with the same rigor as commercial and financial risk
Portfolio leadership gaps are identified and addressed early in the hold period
Critical talent is retained through ownership transitions and organizational change
Sponsors can describe their human capital approach credibly to limited partners and buyers
services.who_we_serve: We work with deal partners, operating partners and heads of portfolio operations at middle-market and growth equity firms, as well as independent sponsors and family offices making control investments. Typical trigger moments include a new platform acquisition, a founder-led business moving to professional management, an underperforming portfolio company, a significant add-on that requires integration, and preparation for a sale process. We also support firms building their first in-house human capital function who want consistent methods across the portfolio.
services.impact_lens: Private equity ownership shapes the working lives of many employees, and the choices sponsors make about leadership, pay, structure and culture ripple outward to customers and communities. Our private equity advisory helps sponsors make those choices with better evidence. Retaining skilled employees, investing in managers and designing fair incentive structures tend to improve service quality and stability for customers. Responsible ownership practices also build trust with communities and limited partners, and they support more durable businesses that continue to perform after exit.

faqs.q: What does a private equity human capital advisor do?
faqs.a: A human capital advisor helps sponsors assess and improve the people side of an investment. That includes evaluating management teams, identifying workforce risks during diligence, building the people workstream of the 100-day plan, supporting leadership hires and organizational change, and tracking people metrics through the hold period. The aim is to make sure the leaders and workforce can deliver the value creation plan, and to surface risks early enough to act on them.

faqs.q: When should a PE firm bring in people advisors during a deal?
faqs.a: Ideally before signing, while there is still time to adjust price, structure or the plan. Pre-close work can be scoped to the access available, often a mix of data room analysis, management sessions and reference conversations. Many sponsors also engage advisors immediately after close to build the 100-day plan, or mid-hold when a portfolio company is underperforming and the root cause appears to be leadership or organizational rather than market-driven.

faqs.q: How is this different from executive search?
faqs.a: Executive search fills specific roles. Our work starts earlier and is broader: we assess whether the current team fits the plan, define what new roles truly require, and address organizational design, incentives and culture around those hires. When search is needed, we help define success profiles and assess finalists, and we can work alongside your preferred search firm. We have no placement fees, so our recommendations are not tied to hiring.

faqs.q: Can you work across an entire portfolio?
faqs.a: Yes. Many operating teams want consistent methods for management assessment, people diligence and people metrics across all portfolio companies. We can design a common toolkit, train deal and operating teams to use it, and provide on-demand support for individual companies. This creates comparable data across the portfolio and helps sponsors identify patterns, such as recurring leadership gaps, that inform future investment decisions.

services.name: Human Capital Due Diligence
services.meta_title: Human Capital Due Diligence for Investors & Acquirers
services.meta_description: Human capital due diligence that assesses leadership, workforce risk, compensation and culture before you sign, with findings tied to your deal model.
services.summary: Pre-signing assessment of leadership, workforce, compensation and culture, with findings translated into deal risks, price considerations and day-one priorities.
services.lede: Human capital due diligence that gives investors and acquirers a clear, evidence-based view of leadership strength, workforce risk and cultural fit before signing, with findings tied directly to valuation and the plan.
challenge: Most deals receive thorough financial, legal and commercial diligence, while the people who will execute the plan receive a few management presentations and a census file. Yet many post-close problems trace back to human factors that were visible, or at least discoverable, before signing: a founder whose relationships hold the customer base together, a compensation structure that cannot survive a change of control, a second layer of management that is thinner than it appears, or an engineering team with a history of quiet attrition.

Diligence timelines are short, access is limited and sellers present the business in its best light. Deal teams need a disciplined way to test people assumptions within those constraints, and to separate material risks from ordinary organizational noise. They also need findings expressed in terms an investment committee can act on: price adjustments, retention requirements, conditions to close, or priorities for the first hundred days. Human capital due diligence provides that discipline and translates it into decisions.

approach.title: Structured management sessions
approach.body: We conduct structured interviews with the CEO and leadership team, focused on how decisions are made, how the team works together and how each leader thinks about the plan. Where permitted, we add conversations with selected second-layer managers and reference sources. We listen for consistency, depth of operating knowledge and where authority truly sits.

approach.title: Data room people analytics
approach.body: We analyze the employee census, payroll, turnover history, compensation and benefits, organization charts and available engagement data. We look for attrition concentrated in critical roles, pay compression or market gaps, key person dependency, unusual spans and layers, and change of control or severance liabilities that affect the deal model.

approach.title: Risk register and deal implications
approach.body: We consolidate findings into a human capital risk register rated by likelihood and impact, with each risk linked to a deal implication: valuation, structure, retention arrangements, earn-out design, representations, or a 100-day action. This gives the investment committee a concise view of what matters and what does not.

approach.title: Retention and day-one planning
approach.body: For risks that must be addressed at close, we help design retention arrangements for critical talent, outline management incentive plan principles and draft day-one communication priorities. Where a leadership change is likely, we define the role requirements and transition approach so that the business does not lose momentum during the ownership change.

approach.title: Handover to the value creation plan
approach.body: Diligence findings should not sit in a binder. We hand over a set of baseline people metrics and open questions to the post-close team, so that the value creation plan builds directly on what diligence revealed and progress can be measured from day one. Nothing learned is lost.

deliverables: Human capital diligence report for the investment committee
Leadership team assessment with individual and collective findings
Workforce analytics summary covering attrition, pay and structure
Human capital risk register with deal implications
Key talent retention recommendations and priorities
Baseline people metrics for post-close tracking
outcomes: Deal teams enter negotiations with a clear understanding of material people risks
Valuation and deal structure reflect leadership and workforce realities, not assumptions
Critical employees are identified and retained through the ownership transition
The post-close team starts with a fact base rather than rebuilding one
services.who_we_serve: Human capital due diligence is commissioned by private equity deal teams, corporate development leaders, family offices and impact investors evaluating control or significant minority investments. It is especially valuable for founder-led businesses, carve-outs from larger corporations, services businesses where talent is the core asset, and cross-border or cross-sector deals where cultural fit is uncertain. Buyers often engage us after a letter of intent is signed and confirmatory diligence begins, though earlier screening is also possible.
services.impact_lens: Ownership changes create real uncertainty for employees, and poorly planned transitions can disrupt livelihoods, customer relationships and local communities. Rigorous human capital due diligence helps buyers anticipate those effects and plan responsibly: identifying fair pay issues before they become legal or reputational problems, recognizing which employees hold customer trust, and planning communication that treats people with respect. Buyers who understand the workforce they are acquiring are better positioned to keep commitments to employees and customers alike.

faqs.q: What is included in human capital due diligence?
faqs.a: Typical scope covers leadership team assessment, workforce demographics and structure, turnover and retention patterns, compensation and benefits benchmarking, incentive and change of control arrangements, HR compliance indicators, and cultural fit or integration risk. Scope is tailored to the deal thesis, so a software business might emphasize engineering retention while a multi-site services business might focus on frontline turnover and labor cost structure.

faqs.q: How long does human capital due diligence take?
faqs.a: Most engagements run in parallel with confirmatory diligence and are scoped to fit the deal timeline, often a few weeks. A focused red flag review can be completed faster when timing is tight. The depth of work depends on data room quality and access to management. We agree on scope and key questions with the deal team at the outset so findings arrive in time to inform the investment committee decision.

faqs.q: Can you assess culture during diligence?
faqs.a: Yes, within the limits of access. We combine management interviews, available survey data, review platform signals, turnover patterns and observation of how the leadership team operates together. We avoid vague labels and instead describe specific cultural characteristics, such as how decisions get made or how performance is managed, that are relevant to the plan or to integration with an existing business.

faqs.q: How do findings affect the deal?
faqs.a: Findings can inform price, structure and planning. Examples include retention or rollover arrangements for key leaders, earn-out terms aligned to people dependencies, specific representations and warranties, conditions related to leadership hires, and priorities for the 100-day plan. Not every finding changes the deal, and part of our job is distinguishing material risks from ordinary issues that any business of similar size would have.

services.name: Value Creation Planning
services.meta_title: Value Creation Planning with a Human Capital Lens
services.meta_description: Value creation planning that links each lever in the investment thesis to the leaders, structure and workforce capabilities needed to deliver it.
services.summary: Value creation plans and 100-day plans that connect each financial lever to the leadership, organization and workforce capabilities required to deliver it.
services.lede: Value creation planning that ties every lever in your investment thesis to the people, roles and capabilities needed to execute it, so the 100-day plan and the full hold period rest on a realistic foundation.
challenge: Value creation plans are usually built from the financial model outward: pricing initiatives, procurement savings, add-on acquisitions, new market entry, operational improvement. Each lever looks sound on a spreadsheet. What is often missing is a rigorous view of who will do the work, whether they have the capacity and capability, and what organizational changes are required. Plans that ask an already stretched leadership team to run five major initiatives simultaneously tend to stall, regardless of the quality of the analysis behind them.

The first hundred days set the tone for the entire hold period. Employees are watching for signals about the new owner, managers are uncertain about their roles, and the leadership team is absorbing new reporting requirements. A value creation plan that ignores this human context can trigger the very attrition and disengagement that undermine it. Sponsors and management teams need plans that are ambitious about outcomes and honest about the people and organizational conditions needed to get there.

approach.title: Test the plan with those who will run it
approach.body: We interview the leadership team, key managers and selected frontline employees about each value creation lever: what it will take, what has been tried before and what might get in the way. These conversations surface execution risks and hidden capacity constraints that do not appear in the financial model.

approach.title: Capacity and capability baseline
approach.body: We map initiatives against the leaders and teams responsible, assess bandwidth and skills gaps, and establish a baseline of people indicators such as turnover in critical roles, manager spans and engagement. This shows where the plan is under-resourced and which capabilities must be hired, built or borrowed.

approach.title: An integrated, sequenced plan
approach.body: We co-design a value creation plan that pairs each lever with named owners, required organizational changes, talent moves and milestones. Initiatives are sequenced to respect change capacity. The 100-day plan sets out early decisions, quick wins and communications, with clear governance for how the sponsor and management will review progress.

approach.title: Program management and enablement
approach.body: We help stand up a value creation office or equivalent governance rhythm, support leaders in launching initiatives, and coach managers on communicating change. Where new roles are created, we help define them and integrate new hires. The emphasis is on building internal capability to run the plan.

approach.title: Leading indicators and course correction
approach.body: We build a dashboard that tracks both financial milestones and the people indicators that predict them, such as hiring velocity for growth roles or retention of key operators. Quarterly reviews use this evidence to adjust priorities before problems show up in the results. Boards see causes, not only results.

deliverables: Integrated value creation plan with people requirements per lever
100-day plan with decisions, owners and communications
Leadership capacity and capability gap analysis
Organizational changes and critical hires roadmap
Value creation governance model and meeting cadence
Dashboard combining financial milestones and people leading indicators
outcomes: Value creation initiatives have clear owners with the capacity to deliver them
The first hundred days build confidence among employees rather than uncertainty
Sponsors and management share one realistic view of priorities and sequencing
Execution risks surface early through leading indicators instead of missed quarters
services.who_we_serve: Our value creation planning clients include private equity operating partners, portfolio company CEOs and CFOs, and boards of sponsor-backed companies. Common trigger moments are the period immediately after close, a change in CEO, a refreshed plan midway through the hold, or an add-on acquisition that changes the shape of the business. We also work with impact investors and family offices who want growth plans that account for employee and community outcomes alongside financial returns.
services.impact_lens: A well-designed value creation plan can raise the quality of work as well as the quality of earnings. When plans account for workload, invest in managers and create clearer roles, employees experience less chaos and more opportunity to grow. Customers benefit from steadier service and fewer disruptions during change. Plans that consider local hiring, fair pay progression and community relationships can also strengthen the places where portfolio companies operate. These outcomes support the financial thesis rather than compete with it.

faqs.q: What is a value creation plan in private equity?
faqs.a: A value creation plan sets out how an investor and management team intend to increase the value of a business during the holding period. It typically covers revenue growth, margin improvement, add-on acquisitions, capital efficiency and organizational strengthening, with milestones, owners and governance. The best plans connect each initiative to the people and capabilities required, because execution capacity is often the binding constraint.

faqs.q: What should a 100-day plan include?
faqs.a: A strong 100-day plan covers early leadership decisions, confirmation of the value creation priorities, key talent retention, reporting and governance changes, quick wins that build credibility, and a communication plan for employees, customers and other stakeholders. It should be specific about owners and dates, and realistic about how much change the organization can absorb while still running the business.

faqs.q: How do you account for people in a value creation plan?
faqs.a: For each initiative, we identify who will lead it, what skills and capacity it requires, which organizational changes it depends on, and which employees are critical to its success. We then compare those requirements with the current organization. Gaps become explicit actions, such as a new hire, a role change, training or retention arrangements, and are tracked like any other milestone.

faqs.q: Can you support a plan that has already been written?
faqs.a: Yes. Many engagements begin with a plan that exists but is not progressing as expected. We review it with the leadership team, diagnose where people and organizational constraints are slowing execution, and recommend adjustments to sequencing, ownership, resourcing or governance. This is often faster and more useful than starting again.

services.name: Post-Merger Integration
services.meta_description: Post-merger integration consulting focused on leadership selection, organization design, culture and retention so combined businesses deliver the deal case.
services.summary: Integration support for acquisitions, mergers and carve-outs, focused on leadership, organization design, culture and retaining the people who carry the deal value.
services.lede: Post-merger integration consulting that puts people at the center: selecting leaders fairly, designing the combined organization, bridging cultures and retaining critical talent so the combined business delivers its deal case.
challenge: Acquisitions are often justified by cost and revenue assumptions that depend on two groups of people learning to work as one. Integration teams typically manage systems, finance and legal workstreams well, while the human questions arrive all at once: who leads which function, which roles change or disappear, whose processes prevail and how decisions will be made. Uncertainty spreads quickly, and the most marketable employees, often the ones the buyer most needs, are the first to take calls from recruiters.

Carve-outs add their own complexity. A business leaving a larger parent must stand up functions it never owned, define its own culture and leadership team, and manage transition service agreements while keeping customers served. Roll-up strategies compound the challenge by repeating integration many times, often with lean teams. In every case, culture clashes, unclear decision rights and poorly handled selection processes erode trust and productivity in ways that rarely appear in integration status reports until value is already lost.

approach.title: Understand both organizations
approach.body: We interview leaders and employees across both organizations, and conduct focus groups in key functions, to understand how each company actually works: how decisions are made, how performance is managed, what people value and what they fear about the deal. This surfaces cultural differences that matter for integration rather than surface-level contrasts.

approach.title: Integration baseline and risk map
approach.body: We compare organization structures, spans and layers, job architectures, compensation and benefits, and retention patterns across both businesses. We identify roles critical to deal value and employees at elevated flight risk. A short pulse survey establishes a baseline for sentiment that we track through integration.

approach.title: Combined organization and ways of working
approach.body: We design the combined organization top down, from leadership structure to functional design, and define decision rights for the integrated business. We develop a fair, transparent selection process for leadership and key roles, harmonization principles for pay and benefits, and a deliberate culture integration plan built with leaders from both sides.

approach.title: Integration management and change
approach.body: We support the integration management office on people workstreams, coordinate leadership selection, prepare managers for difficult conversations and deliver change communications. For carve-outs, we help build standalone functions and leadership. Day one and day one hundred milestones are planned in detail, with attention to how each change lands for employees.

approach.title: Track integration health
approach.body: We monitor retention of critical talent, sentiment, cross-team collaboration and adoption of new processes against the baseline. Integration governance uses this evidence to intervene early. When the formal integration closes, we hand over metrics and ownership to the combined leadership team. Lessons learned inform the next acquisition, which matters for serial acquirers.

deliverables: Cultural assessment comparing both organizations on decision-relevant dimensions
Combined organization design and decision rights framework
Leadership and key role selection process and criteria
Critical talent retention plan with flight risk analysis
Day one and first hundred days people and communications plan
Integration health dashboard tracking retention and sentiment
outcomes: Leaders for the combined organization are selected through a process employees regard as fair
Critical talent stays through integration and contributes to the deal case
Employees understand the new structure, their roles and how decisions are made
Cultural differences are addressed deliberately rather than left to resolve on their own
services.who_we_serve: We support corporate development leaders, chief HR officers, integration management office leads and private equity operating partners. Our post-merger integration work covers strategic acquisitions, mergers of equals, platform and add-on combinations in buy-and-build strategies, and carve-outs from larger parents. Nonprofit and healthcare mergers, where mission alignment and community trust are as important as cost structure, are also a frequent focus. Engagements usually begin between signing and close, though we also help with integrations that have stalled.
services.impact_lens: Integrations affect people deeply: roles change, colleagues leave, familiar ways of working disappear. How a combined organization handles those changes signals what it values. Fair selection, honest communication and thoughtful support for affected employees preserve dignity and trust. Customers experience fewer service disruptions when the people serving them are stable and informed. For mergers involving hospitals, nonprofits or community institutions, careful integration protects access to services that communities depend on, which is a social obligation as well as a business priority.

faqs.q: Why do mergers fail on the people side?
faqs.a: Common causes include delayed or opaque leadership decisions, loss of critical talent during uncertainty, unaddressed differences in how the two organizations make decisions, and integration plans that underestimate the change load on managers. Many of these issues are predictable. Assessing culture and talent risk early, and designing fair processes for selection and harmonization, reduces the chance that people issues erode the value of the deal.

faqs.q: How do you integrate two company cultures?
faqs.a: We start by describing each culture in specific, observable terms, such as how decisions are made, how conflict is handled and how performance is recognized. Leaders from both organizations then agree on which practices the combined business will adopt, which it will retire and which it will build new. These choices are embedded in structures, processes and leadership behavior, not only communicated through values statements.

faqs.q: How is a carve-out different from a typical integration?
faqs.a: In a carve-out, the business must build an independent organization rather than fold into an existing one. That means standing up functions previously provided by the parent, appointing a standalone leadership team, defining a distinct culture and managing transition service agreements. Employees often face uncertainty about their identity and career paths, so clear communication and early leadership decisions are especially important.

faqs.q: When should integration planning begin?
faqs.a: Integration planning ideally begins during diligence, when cultural and talent risks are first assessed, and accelerates between signing and close. Early planning allows leadership decisions to be announced quickly after close, which reduces uncertainty. Where regulatory constraints limit information sharing before close, we use clean team arrangements and plan around what is permissible.

services.name: Impact Investing Advisory
services.meta_title: Impact Investing Advisory for Funds and Foundations
services.meta_description: Impact investing advisory for funds, foundations and family offices: impact theses, diligence, portfolio support and stakeholder-informed measurement.
services.summary: Advice for impact funds, foundations and family offices on impact theses, investment diligence, portfolio support and stakeholder-informed measurement.
services.lede: Impact investing advisory for funds, foundations, family offices and CDFIs that want their capital to improve outcomes for workers, customers and communities, with evidence strong enough to guide decisions and withstand scrutiny.
challenge: Impact investors face a demanding dual mandate. They must generate the financial returns their investors expect while producing social or environmental outcomes that are real, attributable and meaningful to the people they are meant to benefit. Many funds articulate an impact thesis at launch but struggle to apply it consistently in deal selection, to support portfolio companies in deepening impact, or to separate genuine contribution from favorable trends. Without that discipline, impact claims become difficult to defend.

The people whose lives an investment is intended to improve are often absent from the process. Impact theses are written by investors, metrics are chosen for convenience and reporting flows upward to limited partners, rarely back to employees or communities. Meanwhile, expectations from asset owners and regulators continue to rise, and accusations of impact washing carry real reputational cost. Investors need practical ways to bring stakeholder voice into investment decisions and to manage impact with the same seriousness as financial performance.

approach.title: Ground the thesis in stakeholder voice
approach.body: We interview fund leadership, investment committee members and portfolio leaders, and, where appropriate, conduct listening sessions with workers, customers and community members affected by the strategy. This helps confirm whether the intended outcomes match what stakeholders actually need, and where the thesis may rest on untested assumptions.

approach.title: Impact diligence and baselines
approach.body: We help build impact diligence into the investment process, assessing intended outcomes, depth and scale of effect, contribution and risk, using widely recognized dimensions of impact. For existing portfolios, we establish baselines on job quality, access and affordability, or other outcomes central to the thesis.

approach.title: Impact thesis and management system
approach.body: We co-design or refine the fund's theory of change, impact scoring approach, investment committee templates and portfolio engagement model. Where relevant, we help structure impact-linked terms or incentives. Each element is designed to be practical for deal teams and proportionate for portfolio companies with limited reporting capacity.

approach.title: Portfolio support and capability building
approach.body: We work directly with portfolio companies on impact-relevant improvements, such as job quality, inclusive hiring, customer access or community engagement, and train investment teams to apply the impact framework consistently. Support is tailored to company stage and sector. We emphasize practical changes that portfolio leaders can sustain with their own teams and budgets.

approach.title: Reporting and learning
approach.body: We help design LP reporting that is candid about progress and limitations, and internal review processes that feed learning back into future investment decisions. Where useful, we prepare funds for independent verification of their impact management practices. Learning reviews ask what worked, for whom and why, and feed those answers into the next round of investment decisions.

Portfolio companies receive practical support to deepen impact alongside growth
Impact claims are grounded in evidence and stakeholder perspectives rather than assertion
Limited partners receive transparent reporting that includes both progress and shortfalls
services.who_we_serve: We serve impact fund managers, foundation program-related and mission-related investment teams, family offices with impact mandates, community development financial institutions and corporate venture arms with social objectives. Typical trigger moments include launching a new fund, preparing for an LP diligence process, responding to concerns about impact credibility, expanding into a new impact theme, or professionalizing an impact practice that has grown faster than its systems. We also support asset owners evaluating impact managers.
services.impact_lens: Impact investing exists to direct capital toward better outcomes for people and the planet, so the quality of impact management determines whether that purpose is fulfilled. By bringing workers, customers and communities into the design of theses and metrics, our impact investing advisory helps investments respond to real needs. Better job quality in portfolio companies benefits employees and their families. Improved access to essential products and services benefits underserved customers. Honest reporting strengthens trust across the field and helps more capital flow toward what works.

faqs.q: What does an impact investing advisor do?
faqs.a: An impact investing advisor helps investors define what impact they intend to create, assess it during diligence, support portfolio companies in achieving it and measure and report results credibly. Work can include developing a theory of change, designing impact scoring for the investment committee, building stakeholder engagement into the process and preparing reports for limited partners. The goal is to manage impact with the same rigor as financial returns.

faqs.q: How do you avoid impact washing?
faqs.a: Credible impact rests on clear intended outcomes, evidence of contribution, honest reporting of shortfalls and input from affected stakeholders. We help investors define specific outcomes, distinguish their contribution from broader trends, choose indicators that reflect real change for people, and report transparently. Independent verification of impact management practices can provide additional assurance where investors seek it.

faqs.q: Which impact frameworks do you work with?
faqs.a: We work with the frameworks and standards our clients already use or that their limited partners expect, including widely adopted dimensions of impact, sector taxonomies and principles for impact management. We are framework-agnostic and focus on making whichever approach is chosen useful in practice, so that it informs investment and portfolio decisions rather than serving only as a reporting exercise.

faqs.q: Can you help a conventional fund develop an impact strategy?
faqs.a: Yes. Some conventional funds want to launch a dedicated impact vehicle, while others want to integrate impact considerations into an existing strategy. We help assess whether the firm's sourcing, expertise and portfolio support capabilities fit an impact mandate, define a credible thesis, and design the investment process changes required. We are candid when a proposed strategy is unlikely to produce the intended outcomes.

services.name: ESG & Impact Measurement
services.meta_description: ESG and impact measurement consulting that builds credible, decision-useful metrics on workforce, customers and communities for investors and companies.
services.summary: Decision-useful ESG and impact measurement frameworks, with particular depth on social and human capital indicators for investors and portfolio companies.
services.lede: ESG and impact measurement consulting that helps investors and companies build credible, proportionate metrics, with particular depth in the social and human capital indicators that are hardest to measure well.
challenge: Investors and companies face a growing volume of ESG and impact data requests from limited partners, lenders, customers and regulators. Disclosure regimes and industry frameworks differ in scope and definitions, and portfolio companies with lean finance and HR teams often spend significant effort completing questionnaires that produce little insight. Environmental metrics have matured faster than social ones, leaving workforce, community and customer outcomes measured inconsistently or reduced to simple headcounts.

The deeper problem is that much ESG data is collected to satisfy external audiences rather than to improve decisions. Metrics are selected for availability, not relevance. Data quality is uneven across the portfolio, and few organizations can explain how their indicators connect to material risks or to the outcomes they claim. Investors who want measurement that is credible to outside stakeholders and useful to management need a framework grounded in materiality, sensible data practices and the perspectives of the people affected.

approach.title: Clarify purpose and materiality
approach.body: We interview investment teams, portfolio leaders and, where relevant, employees and community stakeholders to understand what decisions measurement should inform and which issues are material. We consider both financial materiality and the impact on people and the environment, the perspective often described as double materiality.

approach.title: Data audit and baselines
approach.body: We audit existing ESG data collection across the fund or company: what is collected, how it is defined, how reliable it is and who uses it. For social indicators such as turnover, pay equity, health and safety, training and employee voice, we establish baselines with clear definitions and documented methods.

approach.title: Proportionate measurement framework
approach.body: We design a core indicator set aligned to applicable frameworks and disclosure regimes, with sector-specific additions where material. Each indicator has a definition, owner, data source and collection frequency. We keep the burden proportionate to company size so that portfolio teams can report reliably without diverting attention from running the business.

approach.title: Roll out data collection and training
approach.body: We implement collection templates or platforms, train portfolio company contacts, and support the first reporting cycle. We help companies interpret their results and identify improvement priorities, so measurement leads to action rather than ending at submission. Early cycles surface data gaps and definitional issues, which we resolve with companies before they become recurring problems.

approach.title: Reporting, assurance readiness and review
approach.body: We build dashboards and report structures for boards, investment committees and limited partners, and prepare data processes for external assurance where required. An annual review refines indicators as frameworks, regulation and portfolio composition change. Changes are made deliberately, so year-over-year comparisons remain meaningful and reporting stays credible to limited partners and other stakeholders.

Core and sector-specific ESG indicator set with definitions
Social and human capital metrics methodology
Data collection templates and portfolio company guidance
Board and limited partner ESG reporting structure
Assurance readiness review of data processes
outcomes: ESG data reflects material issues rather than whatever is easiest to collect
Portfolio companies report consistently with a manageable level of effort
Social and workforce indicators inform management decisions and improvement priorities
Investors can respond confidently to limited partner and regulatory requests
services.who_we_serve: Our ESG and impact measurement work serves private equity and private credit firms, impact funds, family offices, foundations with investment portfolios, and companies preparing for investor or regulatory disclosure. Clients include heads of ESG and sustainability, investor relations leaders, chief financial officers and chief people officers. Engagements are often triggered by a new fundraise, a significant LP questionnaire, new disclosure requirements in a key market, or a recognition that existing ESG reporting is not informing decisions.
services.impact_lens: Measurement shapes attention. When investors and companies measure job quality, fair pay, safety and employee voice with care, those outcomes receive management attention and resources. Good customer and community indicators help companies notice when their products or operations cause harm or exclude people. Proportionate frameworks also respect the time of portfolio teams, many of whom are small. Credible, honest ESG and impact measurement builds trust with stakeholders and helps capital markets reward businesses that serve people well.

faqs.q: What is the difference between ESG and impact measurement?
faqs.a: ESG measurement typically assesses how environmental, social and governance factors affect a company's risk and performance, and how the company manages them. Impact measurement focuses on the outcomes a company or investment produces for people and the planet, including whether those outcomes would have occurred anyway. Many investors need both, and a well-designed framework can serve both purposes with a shared core of indicators.

faqs.q: How do you measure the S in ESG?
faqs.a: Social measurement covers workforce, customers, supply chain and communities. For the workforce, useful indicators include turnover and retention, pay equity, health and safety, training, employee engagement and representation. For customers and communities, indicators depend on the business and might cover access, affordability, product safety or local employment. We combine quantitative data with structured employee and stakeholder input to capture what numbers alone miss.

faqs.q: What is double materiality?
faqs.a: Double materiality considers two perspectives: how sustainability issues affect a company's financial position, and how the company affects people and the environment. Some disclosure regimes require both perspectives. In practice, applying double materiality helps companies identify issues that may not yet affect financial results but matter significantly to employees, communities or ecosystems, and that may become financially material over time.

faqs.q: How do you reduce the ESG reporting burden on portfolio companies?
faqs.a: We start by eliminating indicators that no one uses, aligning definitions across frameworks so one data point can satisfy several requests, and drawing on data the company already holds in payroll, HR and finance systems. We tailor requirements to company size and sector. Clear guidance, templates and a single annual collection cycle also reduce the repeated ad hoc requests that frustrate portfolio teams.

services.name: Portfolio Leadership Assessment
services.meta_title: Portfolio Leadership Assessment for PE Sponsors
services.meta_description: Portfolio leadership assessment that evaluates CEOs and management teams against the value creation plan, with clear actions for sponsors and boards.
services.summary: Evidence-based leadership assessment of portfolio CEOs and management teams against the specific demands of the value creation plan.
services.lede: Portfolio leadership assessment for sponsors and boards who need an objective view of whether the CEO and management team can deliver the plan, and a clear set of development, hiring or succession actions.
challenge: Sponsors routinely cite leadership as one of the most important determinants of portfolio outcomes, yet many still assess management teams informally, through deal team impressions, board meeting performance and reference calls. These signals are useful but incomplete. Leaders who present well may struggle to build teams or make hard operational choices, while quieter leaders may be underestimated. The cost of a delayed leadership change is high, and so is the cost of an unnecessary one.

The question is rarely whether someone is a good executive in general. It is whether this leader, and this team, can deliver this specific plan in this time frame. A founder who built the business to its current scale may or may not be the right person to professionalize it for its next phase. A CFO who managed a stable business may need significant support to run an add-on program and prepare for exit. Sponsors need assessments that answer those specific questions fairly and rigorously.

approach.title: Define what the plan requires
approach.body: We start with the sponsor and board to translate the value creation plan into leadership requirements: the decisions, capabilities and behaviors each role must deliver over the hold period. We then conduct in-depth structured interviews with each executive, exploring their track record, judgment and approach to the challenges ahead.

approach.title: Multi-source evidence
approach.body: We gather confidential input from direct reports, peers and board members, and use validated psychometric tools where appropriate. We review team dynamics by observing leadership meetings and analyzing how decisions flow. Evidence is assessed against the plan-specific requirements, not a generic leadership model. Findings are calibrated across assessors.

approach.title: Individual and team findings
approach.body: We present a clear view of each leader's strengths, risks and development needs, and an assessment of the team as a whole: capability gaps, overlaps, decision-making patterns and bench depth. Recommendations distinguish between development, role change, additional hires and succession planning. Each recommendation states its urgency and its link to plan risk.

approach.title: Feedback and development planning
approach.body: Each executive receives a constructive feedback session and a development plan, which helps make the assessment a tool for growth rather than only evaluation. Where changes are required, we help sponsors plan transitions thoughtfully, including role definitions for new hires and support for leaders moving on.

approach.title: Reassess as the plan evolves
approach.body: We help boards track development progress and revisit the assessment at key milestones, such as after a major add-on or ahead of exit preparation, so leadership capacity keeps pace with the business. Where several portfolio companies are assessed with the same method, sponsors also gain comparable data that reveals recurring leadership patterns across the portfolio and informs future investment decisions.

Individual executive assessment reports with strengths and risks
Leadership team effectiveness and capability gap analysis
Bench strength and succession readiness view
Individual development plans and feedback sessions
Board summary with recommended leadership actions

Leadership gaps are filled before they slow the value creation plan
Boards maintain an ongoing view of bench strength and succession readiness
services.who_we_serve: Our leadership assessment clients include private equity operating partners, talent partners, deal leads and portfolio company boards, as well as family office and impact investors with board representation. Assessments are commonly commissioned shortly after acquisition, when a portfolio company misses plan, ahead of a significant add-on or transformation, before a CEO succession decision, or as part of exit preparation. Some sponsors use our approach as a standard step across every new platform investment.
services.impact_lens: Leadership decisions shape the daily experience of every employee in a portfolio company. Fair, evidence-based leadership assessment reduces the likelihood of abrupt, poorly explained changes at the top, and helps sponsors invest in developing leaders rather than simply replacing them. Strong management teams create better working conditions, more consistent service for customers and steadier employment for communities that depend on local businesses. When transitions are necessary, a thoughtful process treats departing leaders with respect and protects the organization from disruption.

faqs.q: How do private equity firms assess management teams?
faqs.a: Practices vary widely. Some firms rely on deal team judgment and references, while others use structured interviews, multi-rater feedback and psychometric assessment. The most useful assessments evaluate leaders against the specific demands of the value creation plan and examine the team as a whole, not only individuals. Findings should lead to concrete actions: development, role changes, additional hires or succession plans.

faqs.q: Will a leadership assessment unsettle the management team?
faqs.a: It can if handled poorly. We are transparent with executives about the purpose and process, emphasize development as well as evaluation, and provide each leader with constructive feedback. Many executives value an objective view of their strengths and growth areas. The sponsor and board agree in advance how findings will be shared, which builds trust in the process.

faqs.q: Do you use psychometric tests?
faqs.a: Where appropriate, we use validated instruments to add insight on cognitive approach, personality and leadership style. They are one input among several and never the sole basis for a decision. Structured interviews, track record analysis and multi-source feedback carry most of the weight, because they speak more directly to how a leader will handle the plan's actual challenges.

faqs.q: Should the founder remain CEO after investment?
faqs.a: There is no general answer. Many founders lead successfully through institutional ownership, particularly with strong supporting executives and clear governance. Others are better suited to a chair, product or customer-facing role as the business professionalizes. Our assessment considers the founder's capabilities, motivation and fit with the plan, and helps sponsors and founders reach a decision that serves the business.

services.name: Exit Readiness
services.meta_title: Exit Readiness: Leadership, Talent & People Story
services.meta_description: Exit readiness support that strengthens leadership depth, retains key talent and prepares a credible people narrative for buyers and their diligence teams.
services.summary: Preparing portfolio companies for sale by strengthening leadership depth, securing key talent and building an evidence-based people story for buyers.
services.lede: Exit readiness support that prepares your leadership team, workforce data and people narrative for buyer scrutiny, so the business demonstrates durable capability beyond the current owner and management team.
challenge: Buyers increasingly scrutinize human capital during diligence. They want to know whether the management team will stay and can scale, whether key person dependency has been reduced, whether compensation and incentives are sound, and whether the culture will survive another ownership change. Businesses that cannot answer these questions with clean data and a coherent story risk lower valuations, extended diligence, heavier earn-outs or retention demands that shift value away from sellers.

Exit preparation also creates its own people risks. Rumors of a sale unsettle employees, executives with significant equity may begin to disengage, and management bandwidth is consumed by the process while the business still needs to hit its numbers. Leaders who are critical to the equity story may not have retention arrangements that extend past close. Sponsors need to address these risks well ahead of launching a process, while there is still time to build bench strength and evidence of performance.

approach.title: See the business as a buyer will
approach.body: We interview the leadership team, board and selected managers to understand the equity story and how people contribute to it. We anticipate the questions buyers and their advisors are likely to ask about leadership, talent, culture and incentives, and identify where current answers are weak.

approach.title: Vendor-side human capital review
approach.body: We conduct a sell-side human capital review: workforce data quality, attrition trends, compensation benchmarking, incentive and change of control arrangements, key person dependencies and leadership bench depth. This mirrors buyer diligence so issues are found and addressed by the seller first. Each issue is rated by buyer sensitivity.

approach.title: Close gaps and shape the narrative
approach.body: We prioritize fixes that can be completed before launch, such as strengthening the second layer of leadership, formalizing succession plans, cleaning HR data or rebalancing incentives. We help build a factual people narrative for the information memorandum and management presentation, grounded in metrics the business can substantiate.

approach.title: Prepare leaders and protect talent
approach.body: We prepare the management team for diligence sessions on organization and talent, design retention arrangements for critical employees through the transaction, and plan internal communications for the moment the process becomes known. We help leadership balance process demands with running the business. Executives rehearse likely buyer questions.

approach.title: Data room and transition support
approach.body: We organize people data for the data room, support responses to buyer questions and prepare handover materials so the incoming owner inherits a clear view of the organization. This continuity benefits employees and supports a smoother transition. We also help the leadership team set out how the people agenda would continue under new ownership.

Prioritized pre-launch remediation plan for people risks
Leadership bench and succession documentation for buyers
Key employee retention arrangements through the transaction
People and culture narrative for marketing materials
Organized people data and diligence response support
outcomes: Buyers see a leadership team and organization that can perform beyond the current owner
People-related diligence findings are anticipated and addressed well before the sale process launches
Critical employees remain engaged and committed through the sale process
Employees experience the ownership transition with clarity rather than uncertainty
services.who_we_serve: Exit readiness engagements are typically commissioned by private equity sponsors, portfolio company CEOs and CFOs, and boards preparing for a sale, recapitalization or public listing. Founder-owned businesses preparing for an external sale or a transition to employee ownership also use this work. Ideal timing is a year or more before launch, which allows meaningful improvements in leadership depth and data quality, though shorter preparation windows can focus on the highest-priority risks.
services.impact_lens: A sale process can be an unsettling time for employees, who may hear rumors without explanation and worry about their future. Thoughtful exit readiness reduces that uncertainty through clear communication and fair retention arrangements. Building leadership depth and documenting how the business works also protects customers from disruption when ownership changes. For companies considering employee ownership or mission-aligned buyers, preparation helps sellers evaluate options that preserve jobs, culture and community commitments alongside price.

faqs.q: What does exit readiness mean for human capital?
faqs.a: It means the business can show buyers a capable, committed leadership team with depth below it, reduced dependence on any single person, sound incentive and compensation structures, clean workforce data and a healthy culture. It also means having retention arrangements in place for critical employees and a plan for communicating with the workforce once the sale process becomes known.

faqs.q: When should exit preparation start?
faqs.a: Ideally a year or more before a planned process. That window allows time to hire or develop leaders, reduce key person dependency, address compensation issues and build a track record that substantiates the people story. Shorter windows are workable but focus on documentation, data quality, retention arrangements and diligence preparation rather than structural improvements.

faqs.q: What do buyers look for in a management team?
faqs.a: Buyers look for leaders who have delivered results, understand the business deeply and can credibly execute the next owner's plan. They also look for depth below the top team, alignment among leaders, and evidence that key executives intend to stay. Clarity about each leader's role, track record and incentives after the transaction helps buyers assess management risk.

faqs.q: How do you retain key employees during a sale?
faqs.a: Retention starts with identifying who is genuinely critical to value and continuity, then designing arrangements such as transaction bonuses or extended vesting that reward staying through close and beyond. Equally important are honest communication, clear roles during the process and visible leadership. Financial incentives work best when employees also trust how the transition is being managed.

services.name: Leadership Consulting
services.meta_title: Leadership Consulting for Executives and Senior Teams
services.meta_description: Leadership consulting that strengthens executives and leadership pipelines through evidence, clear expectations and development built around real work.
services.summary: Evidence-based leadership consulting to define what good leadership looks like for your strategy and build it across executives and managers.
services.lede: Leadership consulting for organizations that need their leaders to deliver a demanding strategy. We define the leadership your strategy requires, assess the gap, and build capability through development tied to real work.
challenge: Most organizations invest in leadership development, yet many executives remain unsure whether it is working. Programs are often generic, disconnected from strategy and evaluated by participant satisfaction rather than changes in behavior or results. Leadership competency models sit in HR systems but rarely shape who gets promoted. Meanwhile, the demands on leaders keep shifting: hybrid teams, rapid technological change, tighter budgets and higher expectations from employees about fairness, flexibility and purpose.

The result is a familiar pattern. Senior leaders carry too much, middle managers are promoted for technical skill and given little support, and high-potential employees leave because they cannot see a path forward. Leadership becomes a bottleneck to strategy. Organizations need a clear, specific view of what leadership must look like to deliver their strategy, an honest assessment of where they stand, and development that changes how leaders actually behave in their daily work.

approach.title: Connect leadership to strategy
approach.body: We interview executives, board members and a cross-section of managers and employees to understand the strategy, the leadership challenges it creates and how leaders are currently experienced. We pay particular attention to the gap between espoused leadership values and the behaviors that actually get rewarded.

approach.title: Leadership capability baseline
approach.body: We assess current leadership capability using multi-rater feedback, engagement and retention data by manager, promotion patterns and, where useful, network analysis. This shows where leadership strength is concentrated, where it is thin and how leadership quality affects outcomes such as retention and performance. Findings are shared with leaders openly.

approach.title: A leadership framework people use
approach.body: We co-design a concise leadership framework that describes specific, observable behaviors for each level, from first-line manager to executive. We align it with selection, performance management and promotion, and design development journeys that combine learning, coaching, stretch assignments and peer cohorts tied to real business challenges.

approach.title: Development built around real work
approach.body: We deliver leadership programs, facilitate executive offsites and coach senior leaders. Participants work on live strategic problems, which builds capability and advances business priorities simultaneously. We train internal facilitators and HR partners so the organization can sustain the approach. Senior leaders teach in programs, which signals commitment and reinforces the behaviors the framework describes.

approach.title: Measure behavior change
approach.body: We track changes in multi-rater feedback, team engagement, retention and internal mobility to assess whether leadership is improving. Leaders and HR review this evidence together and adjust investment toward what works. Evaluation is planned from the outset with clear comparison points, so results are credible to executives and boards, and we report candidly when programs are not producing the change intended.

deliverables: Leadership requirements linked to strategic priorities
Leadership capability assessment across levels
Leadership framework with observable behaviors by level
Development journeys for executives, senior and first-line leaders
Executive offsite design and facilitation
Leadership effectiveness dashboard and evaluation approach
outcomes: Leaders share a clear, practical understanding of what is expected of them
Promotion and development decisions reflect the leadership the strategy requires
Leadership development produces observable changes in behavior and team outcomes

services.who_we_serve: Our leadership consulting clients include chief executives, chief people officers, heads of talent and leadership development, and boards. We work with growing companies, portfolio businesses, health systems, universities, nonprofits and public agencies. Common triggers include a new strategy that demands different leadership, rapid growth that has outpaced the leadership bench, low engagement scores traced to managers, a new CEO shaping a team, or a leadership program that has not produced results.
services.impact_lens: Leadership quality is one of the strongest influences on how people experience work. Better leaders create teams where people feel respected, understand their purpose and can grow. Those conditions reduce burnout and turnover and allow employees to serve customers with more care. In mission-driven organizations, stronger leadership translates directly into better services for patients, students or communities. Leadership consulting that focuses on fairness and inclusion also widens access to leadership roles for people who have historically been overlooked.

faqs.q: What does a leadership consultant do?
faqs.a: A leadership consultant helps organizations define the leadership they need, assess current capability and build stronger leaders. Work can include developing leadership frameworks, designing development programs, coaching executives, facilitating leadership team sessions and aligning promotion and performance processes with leadership expectations. Good leadership consulting starts from strategy and measures whether leaders actually change how they work.

faqs.q: How do you measure the impact of leadership development?
faqs.a: We look beyond satisfaction surveys to changes in observable behavior, measured through multi-rater feedback before and after development, and to outcomes in leaders' teams, such as engagement, retention, internal mobility and performance. We set up the evaluation design at the start so that comparisons are meaningful, and we are candid when results are mixed.

faqs.q: Do you deliver off-the-shelf leadership programs?
faqs.a: No. We use proven content and methods, but every program is designed around the client's strategy, leadership framework and real business challenges. Participants work on live problems, apply learning between sessions and receive coaching. This takes more design effort than an off-the-shelf program but produces development that is relevant and more likely to transfer to daily work.

faqs.q: How do you develop middle managers?
faqs.a: Middle managers need clear expectations, manageable spans of control, practical skills in coaching and prioritization, and the authority to make decisions. We address both capability and conditions: development in core management skills alongside changes to role design, workload and decision rights. Peer cohorts help managers solve problems together and build networks across the organization.

services.name: Executive Coaching
services.meta_title: Executive Coaching for CEOs and Senior Leaders
services.meta_description: Executive coaching for CEOs and senior leaders, grounded in multi-source feedback, clear goals and the realities of the role, with progress you can see.
services.summary: Confidential executive coaching for CEOs and senior leaders, grounded in multi-source feedback and focused on the specific demands of the role.
services.lede: Executive coaching for CEOs, senior executives and high-potential leaders facing new roles, larger mandates or difficult transitions, grounded in candid feedback and focused on measurable changes in how you lead.
challenge: Senior leaders rarely receive honest feedback. The higher they rise, the more people filter what they hear, and the fewer peers they have with whom to think through difficult decisions. Executives stepping into larger roles, such as a first CEO appointment, a functional leader joining the executive team or a founder leading through institutional investment, often discover that the habits that brought them success now limit them. Without support, they may adapt slowly, at real cost to their teams and organizations.

Organizations also struggle to get value from coaching. Engagements drift without clear goals, the sponsor has little visibility into progress, and coaches with mixed qualifications offer advice disconnected from the business context. Coaching is sometimes used as a remedial last step rather than as an investment in leaders with significant potential. Executives and their sponsors need coaching that is confidential yet accountable, grounded in evidence about how the leader is experienced, and tied to the outcomes the role demands.

approach.title: Understand the leader and the context
approach.body: We begin with conversations with the leader and their sponsor, such as the CEO, board chair or chief people officer, to understand the role, the challenges ahead and what success would look like. We agree on confidentiality boundaries and how progress will be shared. Expectations are written down.

approach.title: Multi-source feedback
approach.body: We gather structured feedback through interviews with direct reports, peers, board members and others who work closely with the leader, often complemented by a validated assessment. This produces a candid, specific picture of strengths, blind spots and how the leader's behavior affects others. The leader receives it in a facilitated session.

approach.title: A focused development plan
approach.body: With the leader, we translate feedback into two or three development goals tied to the demands of the role, each with observable behaviors that colleagues would notice. The plan is shared with the sponsor so expectations are aligned and the organization can support the leader's growth.

approach.title: Regular coaching on real situations
approach.body: Coaching sessions focus on the leader's live challenges: an upcoming board meeting, a difficult team conversation, a restructuring decision. We help the leader prepare, practice, reflect and adjust. Between sessions, the leader applies new approaches and gathers feedback, building durable habits. Sessions can be in person or virtual, with access between sessions for urgent moments.

approach.title: Review progress and hand over
approach.body: At midpoint and close, we gather follow-up feedback from colleagues to assess change. A final review with the sponsor agrees on next steps, so development continues after the engagement through the leader's own practices and support network. That may include peer support, a mentor, ongoing feedback routines or periodic check-ins with the coach.

deliverables: Three-way contracting session with leader and sponsor
Multi-source feedback report with themes and examples
Individual development plan with observable goals
Regular confidential coaching sessions over the engagement
Midpoint and final progress reviews with colleague feedback
