outcomes: Leaders gain an accurate understanding of how they are experienced by others
Executives make the transition into larger or new roles more quickly and confidently
Colleagues observe specific, lasting changes in the leader's behavior and its effect on the team
Sponsors see a clear link between coaching investment and leadership effectiveness
services.who_we_serve: We coach chief executives, executive team members, founders, managing partners, executive directors of nonprofits and senior public officials. Engagements are often sponsored by boards, CEOs, chief people officers or private equity operating partners. Common trigger moments include a promotion or new appointment, onboarding an executive hired from outside, a founder transitioning to a professional CEO role, preparation for succession, a leadership team under strain, or feedback indicating that a strong performer's style is limiting their impact.
services.impact_lens: When senior leaders change how they lead, the effects reach far beyond them. A CEO who listens better, delegates more clearly or handles conflict more constructively shapes the experience of everyone who reports to them, and of those further down the line. That improves retention, reduces stress and creates room for people to contribute fully. Executive coaching for leaders of mission-driven organizations and public agencies can also strengthen services that customers and communities depend on.

faqs.q: What is executive coaching?
faqs.a: Executive coaching is a confidential, one-on-one development relationship between a senior leader and a qualified coach. It focuses on specific goals tied to the leader's role, typically informed by feedback from colleagues. Unlike training, coaching works on the leader's real situations and decisions. Good coaching builds self-awareness, expands the leader's options and produces behavior changes that colleagues notice.

faqs.q: How long does an executive coaching engagement last?
faqs.a: Most engagements run between six and twelve months, with sessions every two to four weeks. That timeframe allows for feedback, goal setting, sustained practice and a follow-up assessment of change. Shorter engagements can support a specific transition, such as the first months in a new role, while longer relationships sometimes suit CEOs who value a consistent thinking partner.

faqs.q: Is executive coaching confidential?
faqs.a: Yes. The content of coaching conversations remains confidential between the leader and coach. At the outset, we agree with the leader and sponsor on what will be shared, typically the development goals and overall progress. This balance protects the trust coaching requires while giving the organization appropriate visibility into its investment.

faqs.q: How do you measure coaching results?
faqs.a: We measure change against the goals agreed at the start, using follow-up feedback from the same colleagues who contributed to the initial assessment. We also consider evidence such as team engagement, retention or progress on business objectives connected to the goals. The sponsor and leader review results together at the end of the engagement.

services.name: Management Consulting
services.meta_title: Management Consulting with a People-First Lens
services.meta_description: Management consulting that solves complex business problems by pairing rigorous analysis with a deep understanding of the people who make the work happen.
services.summary: Rigorous management consulting for complex business problems, pairing structured analysis with insight into the people who will carry out the answer.
services.lede: Management consulting for leaders facing complex problems in performance, growth or organization. We combine structured analysis with deep attention to people, so recommendations are both sound and capable of being carried out.
challenge: Leaders often face problems that cut across functions and resist simple answers: a business that is growing but losing margin, a service organization whose quality varies widely across sites, a public agency asked to deliver more with fewer resources, or a nonprofit whose programs have expanded faster than its operations. Internal teams are busy running the organization and may be too close to the issue to see it clearly. Traditional consulting can provide analytical horsepower, but recommendations often stall because they underestimate the human side of implementation.

Many organizations have experienced consulting projects that produced impressive analysis and little lasting change. The slide deck identified the right answer, but managers were not involved in shaping it, employees did not understand it and the organization lacked the capability to sustain it. Leaders need advisors who bring rigor and independence, and who also understand that the way a solution is developed, and who develops it, largely determines whether it succeeds.

approach.title: Frame the right problem
approach.body: We start by defining the problem precisely with leaders, then test that definition through interviews and site visits with managers, front-line employees and, where relevant, customers. Many engagements change direction at this stage, because the presenting problem is a symptom of something deeper. We also review prior work.

approach.title: Hypothesis-driven analysis
approach.body: We build a fact base using operational, financial, customer and workforce data, testing hypotheses rather than collecting data for its own sake. We look for variation across sites, teams or segments, which often reveals both the root causes of a problem and internal examples of what good looks like.

approach.title: Solutions shaped with the organization
approach.body: We develop options with working teams that include the managers and employees who will carry them out. Options are evaluated against clear criteria, including financial impact, feasibility, risk and effect on employees and customers. Leaders receive a recommendation with explicit trade-offs, not a single answer presented as inevitable.

approach.title: Implementation with internal owners
approach.body: We support implementation through pilots, detailed planning, project management and change support. Internal owners lead each workstream with our support, building the capability to continue after we leave. We adapt the plan as pilots reveal what works in practice. Steering committees review progress and decide on adjustments with clear evidence in hand.

approach.title: Embed and hand over
approach.body: We establish performance measures, governance routines and documentation so that improvements become standard practice. A structured handover ensures internal teams own the results and know how to respond if performance drifts. We also document the methods used, such as root cause analysis and pilot design, so internal teams can apply the same disciplined problem solving to the next challenge without outside support.

Fact base drawing on operational, financial and workforce data
Options assessment with explicit trade-offs and criteria
Recommendation and implementation roadmap
Pilot design, results and scale-up plan
Performance measures and governance for sustaining results

Recommendations reflect the knowledge of the people closest to the work
Implementation progresses steadily because internal owners helped shape the solution from the start

services.impact_lens: Management decisions about structure, process and resources shape the working lives of employees and the experiences of customers. Our management consulting approach involves the people affected and weighs the human consequences of each option alongside financial ones. That reduces the risk of improvements that cut costs while degrading service or burning out staff. For public agencies and nonprofits, better management translates into more effective services for the communities they serve, which is the ultimate test of good advice.

faqs.q: What does a management consultant do?
faqs.a: A management consultant helps leaders solve complex problems related to strategy, operations, organization and performance. Work typically involves defining the problem, gathering and analyzing data, developing and evaluating options, recommending a course of action and supporting implementation. The value lies in independent perspective, structured problem solving and the ability to bring experience from other organizations.

faqs.q: How is your management consulting different?
faqs.a: We place equal weight on analytical rigor and on the people who will carry out the answer. We involve managers and employees in shaping solutions, assess the human impact of each option and build internal capability during the engagement. This approach is grounded in the belief that how a solution is developed strongly affects whether it is adopted and sustained.

faqs.q: Do you work with nonprofits and government agencies?
faqs.a: Yes. Mission-driven and public organizations face many of the same management challenges as companies, often with tighter resources and more complex stakeholder environments. We adapt our methods to those contexts, including governance structures, funding constraints and public accountability requirements, and we consider community outcomes as a central measure of success.

faqs.q: How long does a typical engagement take?
faqs.a: Duration depends on scope. A focused diagnostic can take several weeks, while a full engagement from diagnosis through implementation support may run several months. We often structure work in phases with decision points, so leaders can confirm the direction before committing to implementation and adjust scope as the problem becomes clearer.

services.name: Organizational Design
services.meta_title: Organizational Design Consulting: Structure That Works
services.meta_description: Organizational design consulting covering structure, spans and layers, decision rights and roles, co-designed with your people to support your strategy.
services.summary: Organizational design consulting covering structure, spans and layers, decision rights and roles, built from strategy and tested with your people.
services.lede: Organizational design consulting that aligns structure, roles, spans of control and decision rights with your strategy, using evidence about how work really flows and the input of people who do it.
challenge: Organizations grow by accretion. Teams are added to address new priorities, managers are promoted to retain talent, and reporting lines shift around individuals rather than strategy. Over time, the structure accumulates layers, uneven spans of control, duplicated functions and unclear accountabilities. Decisions slow down because too many people must agree, while important work falls between teams. Employees experience this as frustration, rework and a sense that no one owns the problems they care about.

Restructuring is often treated as the fix, but redrawing boxes on an org chart rarely solves underlying issues. Reorganizations can be disruptive, consume leadership attention and cause talented people to leave, especially when the rationale is unclear or the process feels unfair. Leaders need organizational design grounded in strategy and evidence, attentive to how work actually flows, explicit about decision rights, and implemented in a way that maintains trust and continuity.

approach.title: Start from strategy and pain points
approach.body: We clarify the strategic priorities the organization must support and the design criteria leaders will use to judge options. Interviews and workshops with leaders, managers and employees surface where work gets stuck, where accountability is unclear and where collaboration is difficult. These pain points become explicit tests for any design.

approach.title: Structural diagnostic
approach.body: We analyze spans and layers, role distribution, cost by function, and decision-making patterns. Organizational network analysis shows how information and collaboration actually flow, often revealing informal structures that differ from the formal chart. This evidence grounds design choices in fact rather than assumption. Costs are compared by function and level.

approach.title: Options, decision rights and roles
approach.body: We develop structural options, such as functional, divisional, matrix or hybrid models, and assess them against agreed criteria. We define decision rights using tools like RACI or similar frameworks, clarify accountabilities, and design key roles. Managers and employees test the design to identify issues before implementation.

approach.title: Transition with care
approach.body: We plan the transition in detail: sequencing, role mapping, fair selection processes where needed, and communication at every level. We support leaders through difficult conversations and help teams establish new ways of working, including handoffs, forums and governance routines. Employees know where they stand before changes take effect, which reduces anxiety and rumor.

approach.title: Review and refine
approach.body: We track indicators such as decision speed, role clarity, spans and retention after the change, and conduct a structured review within months of go-live. Designs are refined based on evidence, and governance ensures the structure does not drift back to old patterns. Leaders own the reviews.

Spans and layers and structural cost diagnostic

services.impact_lens: Organizational structure shapes daily work in ways employees feel immediately: who they report to, whether they can make decisions, how often they wait on others and whether their contributions are visible. Good organizational design reduces frustration and burnout and gives people roles they can succeed in. Customers benefit from clearer ownership of their needs and faster responses. Designing changes with employees, and handling transitions fairly, also preserves trust during a period that can otherwise feel threatening.

faqs.q: What is organizational design?
faqs.a: Organizational design is the process of shaping an organization's structure, roles, processes, decision rights and governance so that it can carry out its strategy. It goes beyond the org chart to include how work flows between teams, how decisions are made, how people are measured and rewarded, and how the organization adapts. Good design starts from strategy and is tested against how work really happens.

faqs.q: What is the ideal span of control?
faqs.a: There is no single ideal. Appropriate spans depend on the complexity and variety of work, how experienced team members are, how much coordination is required and how much of a manager's time goes to their own individual work. Routine operational teams can support wider spans, while complex or highly varied work needs narrower ones. We analyze current spans against these factors rather than applying a universal target.

faqs.q: How do you clarify decision rights?
faqs.a: We identify the decisions that matter most to strategy and performance, then define who recommends, who decides, who must be consulted and who needs to be informed. Frameworks such as RACI help structure the conversation, but the real value comes from leaders agreeing explicitly on ownership and holding to those agreements. We test decision rights against real scenarios before finalizing them.

faqs.q: How do you reduce disruption during a reorganization?
faqs.a: Disruption is reduced by a clear rationale, fair processes, fast decisions on leadership roles, honest communication and support for managers who must explain changes to their teams. We sequence changes carefully, protect critical customer-facing work and identify key talent at risk. Involving employees in testing the design also surfaces practical problems early and builds understanding.

services.name: Change Management
services.meta_title: Change Management Consulting Built on Evidence
services.meta_description: Change management consulting that helps people adopt new strategies, systems and structures, with adoption measured through evidence rather than launch dates.
services.summary: Change management that helps employees understand, adopt and sustain new strategies, systems and ways of working, with adoption measured through evidence.
services.lede: Change management consulting that helps organizations bring people through major transitions, from new systems and structures to new strategies, by designing change with them and measuring real adoption rather than activity.
challenge: Organizations change constantly: new technology platforms, restructurings, mergers, policy shifts, return-to-office decisions, new service models and the adoption of AI tools. Each initiative may be sensible on its own, but employees experience them together, often with limited explanation and little say. Change fatigue sets in, cynicism grows, and even well-designed initiatives struggle to win commitment. Leaders see delays, workarounds and declining engagement without always understanding why. Often the problem is not the change itself but how it was introduced.

Many change efforts focus on communication and training plans that are produced near the end of a project, after key decisions have been made. They track activity, such as emails sent or courses completed, rather than whether people have actually changed how they work. Managers, who carry most of the burden of explaining change, are rarely prepared for that role. Organizations need change management that starts early, involves the people affected, equips managers and measures adoption honestly.

approach.title: Understand how change will land
approach.body: We conduct interviews and focus groups with groups affected by the change to understand their concerns, current workload, past experiences of change and what would make the transition workable. This reveals resistance that is rooted in legitimate practical issues, which often improves the change itself.

approach.title: Impact assessment and readiness baseline
approach.body: We assess the impact of the change on each group: what changes in their roles, processes, tools and behaviors, and how significant each shift is. We measure readiness and identify concurrent initiatives to gauge change load. This shapes where to focus effort and how to sequence.

approach.title: Change strategy designed with stakeholders
approach.body: We design a change strategy covering sponsorship, stakeholder engagement, communication, training and reinforcement, tailored to each affected group. Representatives from those groups help shape the approach. We build a change network of respected employees who provide feedback and support peers. Each group's plan reflects how much its work actually changes, avoiding a uniform approach that over-serves some and under-serves others.

approach.title: Equip leaders and managers
approach.body: We coach sponsors on visible leadership, prepare managers with practical guides for team conversations, and deliver communications and training timed to when people need them. We run feedback loops during rollout to identify issues quickly and adjust the plan. Sponsors hear directly from the front line through regular feedback sessions and visible follow-up.

approach.title: Measure adoption and reinforce
approach.body: We track adoption through behavioral and operational indicators, such as system usage, process compliance and outcome measures, alongside sentiment. Reinforcement mechanisms, including recognition, performance expectations and removal of old workarounds, help new ways of working become the norm. Leaders review the evidence on a regular cadence and act where adoption is lagging.

Change readiness baseline and change load analysis
Change strategy and integrated engagement plan
Manager toolkits for leading team conversations
Change network design and enablement
Adoption dashboard tracking behavior and sentiment

services.who_we_serve: Our change management consulting supports transformation leaders, chief information officers, chief people officers, project sponsors and program management offices. Typical initiatives include enterprise technology implementations, restructurings, mergers and integrations, new operating models, new service delivery approaches in health and public services, and responsible adoption of AI tools. We work with companies, public agencies and nonprofits, and we often join programs already underway when adoption has fallen behind plan.
services.impact_lens: Change done poorly takes a real toll: stress, lost confidence, disrupted relationships with customers and, in public services, disruption to people who depend on them. Change done well respects people's time, knowledge and concerns. By involving employees in shaping change and equipping managers to support their teams, we help organizations reduce unnecessary disruption. Customers and communities experience steadier service through transitions, and employees build confidence that future changes will be handled fairly.

faqs.q: What is change management?
faqs.a: Change management is the structured approach to helping people adopt new ways of working, whether those involve technology, processes, structures or strategy. It covers understanding how the change affects different groups, building leadership sponsorship, engaging stakeholders, communicating, training and reinforcing new behaviors. Its purpose is to ensure an initiative's intended benefits are realized through actual adoption.

faqs.q: Why do change initiatives fail?
faqs.a: Common reasons include unclear rationale, weak or inconsistent sponsorship, too many concurrent changes, limited involvement of the people affected, underprepared managers and a focus on launch rather than adoption. Many of these are avoidable when change management begins early, alongside the design of the initiative, rather than being added after decisions have been made.

faqs.q: How do you measure change adoption?
faqs.a: We define what adoption looks like in observable terms for each group, such as using a new system for specific tasks or following a new process. We track these behaviors through operational data where possible, supplemented by pulse surveys and manager feedback. Combining behavior and sentiment indicators gives a more accurate picture than training completion or communication metrics.

faqs.q: How do you prevent change fatigue?
faqs.a: We map all concurrent initiatives affecting each group to understand cumulative change load, then work with leaders to sequence, combine or pause initiatives where load is too high. We also make change easier to absorb through clear explanations, adequate time for learning and removal of old tasks. Listening to employees regularly helps identify fatigue before it becomes disengagement.

services.name: Culture Transformation
services.meta_description: Culture transformation consulting that defines the culture your strategy needs in observable terms and changes the systems and behaviors that shape it.
services.summary: Culture transformation that names the behaviors your strategy needs and changes the systems, leadership habits and routines that shape them.
services.lede: Culture transformation consulting that moves beyond values statements to change how people actually behave, by diagnosing current culture with evidence and redesigning the systems, rituals and leadership habits that shape it.
challenge: Culture is often described as the way things are done when no one is watching, and leaders frequently recognize that their current culture does not support their strategy. A company pursuing innovation may have a culture that punishes failure. A health system focused on safety may find staff hesitant to speak up. An organization committed to inclusion may see that only certain voices shape decisions. Leaders sense these gaps but struggle to describe them precisely or to know where to begin.

Many culture initiatives start with new values, launched through events and posters, and fade within months because nothing else changes. Employees notice when stated values conflict with who gets promoted, how budgets are allocated and how leaders respond to bad news. Culture is shaped by systems, incentives, routines and leadership behavior, and it changes only when those change. Organizations need a disciplined approach that treats culture as something that can be measured, designed and managed over time.

approach.title: Ethnographic culture diagnostic
approach.body: We conduct interviews, focus groups and observation across levels and locations, paying attention to stories people tell, behaviors that are rewarded and the unwritten rules that shape decisions. This qualitative work reveals the culture as employees experience it, including subcultures that differ across teams or sites.

approach.title: Quantify the culture
approach.body: We complement qualitative insight with a culture survey, analysis of existing engagement data, and indicators such as promotion patterns, turnover and speak-up rates. This allows leaders to see where culture differs across groups and to track change over time against a clear baseline. Results are compared across sites.

approach.title: Define target behaviors and levers
approach.body: With leaders and employee co-design teams, we define a small set of culture shifts in observable, behavioral terms. We then identify the levers that will reinforce those behaviors: leadership routines, decision processes, performance and reward systems, onboarding, rituals and symbols. Every lever has an accountable leader and a clear first step that employees will notice.

approach.title: Change systems and leader behavior
approach.body: We help leaders model target behaviors visibly, redesign processes and policies that conflict with the desired culture, and support teams in adopting new routines. Culture champions across the organization test changes locally and share what works, so transformation spreads through practice rather than slogans. Early visible changes build credibility.

approach.title: Track and reinforce
approach.body: We establish a culture dashboard combining survey indicators with behavioral and operational measures. Regular reviews with leadership assess progress, identify where the culture is shifting and where it is stuck, and adjust interventions. Culture transformation is a multi-year effort, and governance keeps it on the agenda.

Culture baseline survey and analysis by group
Target culture shifts defined in observable behaviors
Culture levers roadmap covering systems, routines and leadership

Triggers often include a new strategy, a crisis or reputational event, poor engagement results, persistent turnover or a leadership transition that opens space for change.
services.impact_lens: Culture determines whether people feel safe to speak up, treated fairly and able to do their best work. A healthier culture reduces burnout, harassment and exclusion, and helps organizations retain people who might otherwise leave. Customers notice culture in the quality and consistency of service. In healthcare and public services, cultures that encourage speaking up about risks help protect patients and communities. Culture transformation that is honest and evidence-based creates workplaces that serve both people and performance.

faqs.q: How do you change organizational culture?
faqs.a: Culture changes when the behaviors leaders model, the systems that reward people and the routines that shape daily work all change together. We start by diagnosing current culture with evidence, define a small number of target shifts in behavioral terms, and then change the levers that reinforce them, such as decision processes, performance management and leadership habits. Progress is measured and reviewed over time.

faqs.q: How long does culture transformation take?
faqs.a: Meaningful culture change usually takes several years, though early shifts can be visible within months when leaders change their own behavior and remove obvious contradictions. We structure transformation in phases, with clear indicators of progress at each stage, so leaders can see whether the effort is working and sustain commitment over the necessary time frame.

faqs.q: Can culture be measured?
faqs.a: Yes, though no single measure captures it fully. We combine culture surveys focused on specific behaviors, analysis of engagement data, operational indicators such as promotion patterns and speak-up rates, and qualitative research. Tracking these over time and across groups gives leaders a reliable picture of where culture is changing and where it is not.

faqs.q: What role does psychological safety play in culture?
faqs.a: Psychological safety, the shared belief that it is safe to take interpersonal risks such as raising concerns or admitting mistakes, is foundational to learning, innovation and quality. Research, including Amy Edmondson's work, has highlighted its importance in teams. We often assess psychological safety as part of a culture diagnostic and help leaders build the behaviors that strengthen it.

services.name: Succession Planning
services.meta_title: Succession Planning Consulting for CEOs and Leaders
services.meta_description: Succession planning consulting for CEO and critical roles: success profiles, objective bench assessment, development plans and fair, transparent processes.
services.summary: CEO and leadership succession planning that builds ready benches for critical roles through clear success profiles, objective assessment and targeted development.
services.lede: Succession planning consulting for boards and executive teams who want ready successors for the CEO and critical roles, built on clear success profiles, objective assessment of internal talent and deliberate development.
challenge: Leadership transitions are among the riskiest moments in an organization's life, yet many boards and executive teams lack credible succession plans. Plans may exist on paper, listing names next to roles, but they often rest on informal impressions, favor candidates who resemble current leaders and overlook talent below the senior team. When a CEO departs unexpectedly or a critical executive resigns, the organization discovers that its bench is thinner than assumed and turns to an external search under time pressure.

Succession planning is also sensitive. Incumbents may be reluctant to discuss their departure, high-potential candidates may leave if they cannot see a path forward, and processes that feel opaque can damage trust. Boards need to fulfill their responsibility for CEO succession without destabilizing the current leadership. Organizations need succession planning that is rigorous, fair and forward-looking, designed around what future roles will require rather than what current incumbents do today.

approach.title: Define future role requirements
approach.body: We interview board members, the CEO and executives to understand strategic direction and what future leaders will need to deliver. For each critical role, we develop a success profile describing the experiences, capabilities and attributes required, looking ahead to the organization's next phase rather than backward at the incumbent.

approach.title: Objective bench assessment
approach.body: We assess internal candidates against the success profiles using structured interviews, multi-rater feedback and, where appropriate, validated assessments. We map readiness levels, such as ready now or ready in a few years, and analyze the diversity and depth of each bench, including risks where single candidates or none exist.

approach.title: Succession plan and development
approach.body: We build succession plans for each critical role, with targeted development for each candidate: stretch assignments, broader exposure, coaching and board visibility. We design emergency succession arrangements and define when external benchmarking or search should complement internal candidates. Plans also address knowledge transfer, the relationships successors must build and how candidates will be told about their development without implied promises.

approach.title: Development and transition support
approach.body: We support candidates through development, including coaching and assignment design, and help boards run CEO selection processes when the time comes. For transitions, we plan the handover, the onboarding of the new leader and the role of the departing executive, so continuity is preserved. Departing leaders are supported thoughtfully.

approach.title: Regular talent reviews
approach.body: We establish an annual or semiannual talent review process for the board and executive team, with metrics such as bench coverage, readiness progress and internal fill rates. This keeps succession a living process rather than a document reviewed once and forgotten. Calibration sessions help reduce bias in readiness ratings.

Internal candidate assessments and readiness mapping
Succession plans with bench depth and risk analysis
Individual development plans for succession candidates
Emergency succession protocol for the board
Talent review process and succession metrics

services.impact_lens: Thoughtful succession planning protects the people who depend on an organization. Employees experience less disruption when leadership transitions are well prepared, customers see continuity in relationships and service, and communities that rely on hospitals, universities or major employers benefit from stability. Planning ahead for transitions honors the organization's mission by ensuring it outlasts any single leader.

faqs.q: What is succession planning?
faqs.a: Succession planning is the process of identifying and developing people to fill critical leadership roles when they become vacant. It involves defining what each role will require in the future, assessing internal candidates, creating development plans to close readiness gaps and preparing for both planned and emergency transitions. Effective succession planning is ongoing rather than a one-time exercise.

faqs.q: What is the board's role in CEO succession?
faqs.a: Boards are responsible for ensuring there is a credible plan for CEO succession, both for planned transitions and emergencies. That includes agreeing on the future leadership profile, overseeing assessment and development of internal candidates, deciding whether to consider external candidates and ultimately selecting the next CEO. Boards should review succession regularly, not only when a transition is imminent.

faqs.q: How far in advance should CEO succession planning begin?
faqs.a: Ideally, succession planning is continuous, with a meaningful plan in place several years before an expected transition. That timeframe allows internal candidates to gain the experience they need and gives the board time to evaluate them. An emergency succession plan should exist at all times, regardless of the expected timing of the CEO's departure.

faqs.q: How do you make succession planning fair and inclusive?
faqs.a: We use success profiles tied to future needs rather than the incumbent's style, structured assessment methods that reduce bias, and calibration sessions that challenge assumptions. We look deeper into the organization for potential candidates and examine whether development opportunities are distributed fairly. Transparent criteria help candidates understand how decisions are made.

services.name: Board Advisory & Governance
services.meta_description: Board advisory and governance consulting: board evaluations, composition and skills matrices, committee design and stronger oversight of people and culture.
services.summary: Board evaluations, composition planning and governance design that strengthen board oversight of strategy, leadership succession, people, culture and stakeholder impact.
services.lede: Board governance consulting for corporate, nonprofit and sponsor-backed boards that want to strengthen oversight, improve how they work together and govern people, culture and stakeholder impact with the same rigor as financial performance.
challenge: Boards are expected to oversee more than ever: strategy, risk, executive performance, culture, workforce issues, cybersecurity, sustainability and stakeholder relationships. Yet many boards spend most meeting time on backward-looking reports and compliance items, leaving limited room for strategic discussion. Board composition may not reflect the skills the organization now needs, committee responsibilities can overlap or leave gaps, and the relationship between the board and management may be either too distant or too operational.

Human capital and culture oversight is a particular gap. Boards often receive limited workforce data beyond headcount and engagement scores and may learn of cultural problems only when they become public. Nonprofit boards face additional challenges around fundraising expectations, role clarity and recruitment, while boards of sponsor-backed companies must balance investor priorities with independent oversight. Boards need practical, candid support to assess how well they work and to govern the issues that matter most.

approach.title: Confidential board interviews
approach.body: We interview each director and key executives confidentially about board effectiveness, dynamics, information quality, agenda focus and the board-management relationship. This surfaces candid perspectives that rarely emerge in the boardroom and identifies differences in how directors view their role. All input is reported in aggregate to protect confidentiality.

approach.title: Board evaluation and governance review
approach.body: We complement interviews with a structured board evaluation survey, observe board and committee meetings, and review charters, agendas, board materials and governance documents. We assess composition against a skills matrix tied to strategy and compare governance practices with recognized standards for the organization's sector. Findings are benchmarked against peers.

approach.title: Governance improvements
approach.body: We recommend changes to board composition, committee structure and charters, agenda design, board materials and the delegation of authority between board and management. We help design oversight of people and culture, including the metrics the board should receive and how often they should discuss them.

approach.title: Facilitate and implement
approach.body: We facilitate board retreats and feedback discussions, support director recruitment with defined profiles, design onboarding for new directors and help management improve board reporting. For nonprofit boards, we clarify roles, expectations and the board's relationship with the executive director. Board materials are redesigned to focus on decisions and insight rather than volume.

approach.title: Regular evaluation and development
approach.body: We help the board establish a regular evaluation cycle, an annual governance calendar and ongoing director education on topics such as human capital oversight and stakeholder impact. This makes board effectiveness a continuous practice rather than an occasional review. Periodic external facilitation keeps the evaluation candid and the board accountable to its own commitments.

services.impact_lens: Boards set the tone for how an organization treats its people, customers and communities. When boards oversee culture, workforce practices and stakeholder outcomes thoughtfully, those issues receive sustained attention from management. Well-functioning nonprofit and public boards help organizations deliver on their missions and use resources responsibly. Diverse, well-informed boards are better equipped to anticipate how decisions will affect different groups. Good governance protects the organization's long-term health and the trust that employees and communities place in it.

faqs.q: What is a board evaluation?
faqs.a: A board evaluation is a structured assessment of how effectively a board and its committees fulfill their responsibilities. It typically examines composition, structure, processes, information quality, dynamics and the board-management relationship. Evaluations may use surveys, confidential interviews and meeting observation. An independent facilitator often draws out more candid input and offers an external perspective on governance practices.

faqs.q: How should boards oversee human capital and culture?
faqs.a: Boards should define which workforce and culture issues are material to strategy and risk, receive regular metrics such as turnover in critical roles, engagement, safety, pay equity and succession readiness, and discuss them with management in depth. Many boards assign this oversight to a compensation or people committee with a broadened charter. Directors may also gain insight through site visits and conversations beyond the executive team.

faqs.q: What is a board skills matrix?
faqs.a: A board skills matrix maps the expertise, experience and perspectives the board needs against what current directors bring. It helps identify gaps, guide recruitment and plan for director succession. A useful matrix is tied to the organization's strategy and risks rather than a generic list, and it is updated as strategy and board composition change.

faqs.q: Do you work with nonprofit boards?
faqs.a: Yes. Nonprofit boards face distinct challenges, including clarifying the board's role relative to staff, setting fundraising expectations, recruiting directors with relevant skills and lived experience, and overseeing mission impact. We help nonprofit boards evaluate their effectiveness, clarify roles and responsibilities, strengthen the partnership with the executive director and govern mission outcomes.

services.name: Team Effectiveness
services.meta_title: Team Effectiveness Consulting for Leadership Teams
services.meta_description: Team effectiveness consulting for leadership and critical teams: clearer purpose, decision rights and trust, built on diagnostics and real work sessions.
services.summary: Team effectiveness work for leadership teams and critical cross-functional teams, building clarity of purpose, sound decision-making and trust.
services.lede: Team effectiveness consulting for leadership teams and critical cross-functional teams that need to make better decisions together, work through tension productively and deliver shared priorities rather than parallel agendas.
challenge: Many senior teams are groups of capable individuals rather than teams. Each executive runs their function well, but the team spends meeting time on updates rather than decisions, avoids difficult conversations and leaves cross-functional problems unresolved. Members may agree in the room and act differently afterward. These dynamics are rarely discussed openly, yet employees feel them through conflicting priorities, slow decisions and signals that leaders are not aligned. The cost is slower execution and lost confidence.

Cross-functional teams face similar challenges with less authority. Product teams, transformation programs, clinical units and project teams must coordinate across reporting lines, often with unclear decision rights and competing incentives. Hybrid and distributed work adds complexity. Generic team-building events can create goodwill but rarely change how a team operates. Teams need a clear diagnosis of what is limiting their effectiveness and practical changes to purpose, structure, routines and relationships. The work must change, not only the mood.

approach.title: Individual interviews
approach.body: We interview each team member and selected stakeholders who work with the team, exploring purpose, priorities, decision-making, meeting quality, trust and how conflict is handled. Confidential conversations surface views members may not share in the group, including perceptions of the leader's role. All input is reported in themes, not by name.

approach.title: Team diagnostic
approach.body: We use a validated team effectiveness survey and observe the team in action, often in its regular meetings. Where useful, we analyze meeting time allocation and decision flow. Findings show how the team rates itself on key conditions for effectiveness, such as clear purpose, right membership, psychological safety and supportive context.

approach.title: Team charter and operating rhythm
approach.body: In facilitated working sessions, the team agrees on its shared purpose and priorities, which decisions belong to the team versus individuals, and how it will work together, including meeting design, norms for debate and commitments to each other. The output is a practical team charter, not an abstract values list.

approach.title: Work on real issues
approach.body: We facilitate sessions where the team applies new practices to its actual agenda: making a difficult resource decision, resolving a cross-functional conflict or setting annual priorities. We coach the team leader and give real-time feedback on dynamics, helping new habits take hold. Sessions are short, focused and regular.

approach.title: Pulse checks and team reviews
approach.body: We conduct brief pulse surveys and periodic team reviews to track progress against the baseline. The team learns to review its own effectiveness regularly, so improvement continues as membership and priorities change. We equip the team leader to facilitate these reviews independently, including how to raise difficult topics and renegotiate commitments, so the practice continues without outside facilitation as the team evolves.

deliverables: Confidential team interviews and stakeholder perspectives
Team effectiveness diagnostic report
Team charter covering purpose, priorities and decision rights
Redesigned meeting cadence and agenda structures
Facilitated working sessions on live business issues
Team leader coaching and progress pulse surveys
outcomes: The team shares clear priorities and acts on them consistently
Meetings focus on decisions and problem solving rather than updates
Members raise disagreements openly in the room and resolve them constructively together
Employees experience more consistent direction and fewer conflicting demands from the team
services.who_we_serve: Team effectiveness work serves CEOs and their executive teams, functional leadership teams, newly formed teams after a reorganization or merger, private equity portfolio management teams, clinical and operational leadership groups in health systems, and cross-functional program teams. Common triggers include a new leader forming a team, a team integrating new members, visible tension or misalignment, a demanding strategy that requires joint ownership, or feedback from employees that leaders send mixed messages.
services.impact_lens: Teams at the top of an organization set the conditions for everyone else. When leadership teams align on priorities, make clear decisions and model respectful disagreement, employees face fewer conflicting demands and more coherent direction. Psychological safety within teams supports learning and helps people raise concerns early, which protects customers and, in fields like healthcare, patient safety. Effective cross-functional teams also deliver better experiences for customers whose needs span organizational boundaries.

faqs.q: What makes a team effective?
faqs.a: Research on team effectiveness consistently points to a few conditions: a compelling shared purpose, the right membership, clear roles and decision rights, sound norms for how the team works, a supportive organizational context and psychological safety. Teams that have these conditions in place tend to perform better. Our team effectiveness work diagnoses which conditions are weak and helps the team strengthen them.

faqs.q: How is this different from team building?
faqs.a: Team building events typically focus on relationships and goodwill and are often disconnected from the team's actual work. Team effectiveness work addresses purpose, decision rights, meeting design and how the team handles real issues, alongside trust and relationships. We work on the team's live agenda so improvements carry directly into how the team operates.

faqs.q: How do you help a leadership team that does not trust each other?
faqs.a: Low trust often has specific causes, such as unclear decision rights, competing incentives, past conflicts or inconsistent behavior. We identify those causes through confidential interviews, then help the team address them directly in facilitated conversations. Trust builds when members make and keep explicit commitments to each other, which we help the team practice and review over time.

faqs.q: How long does a team effectiveness engagement take?
faqs.a: A typical engagement runs several months, beginning with a diagnostic, followed by a series of working sessions and periodic follow-up. Some teams start with a single offsite and then continue with quarterly sessions. Sustained work over time produces more durable change than a single event, because new practices need repetition to become habits.
